content: Identifying and treating sexually transmitted infections (STIs) involves recognizing specific syndromes (symptoms reported by the patient) and clinical signs (observable indicators of infection) that are associated with well-defined causes. While an etiological diagnosis is ideal, it is not always feasible due to limitations in accessibility or cost. The 2003 WHO guidelines for managing STIs provide clinical recommendations for syndromic management of urethral discharge and persistent or recurrent urethral discharge. These guidelines emphasize the importance of addressing STIs due to their significant health, social, and economic consequences, as well as their role in increasing the risk of HIV transmission. Molecular-based diagnostic tests, such as nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), are highly accurate and enable targeted treatment. However, these tests are expensive and often unavailable in many settings. Syndromic management, while less precise, remains a practical approach in resource-limited environments. A systematic review revealed that the odds of Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis infection among men with urethral discharge are approximately 10 times higher than among men without discharge. Similarly, Mycoplasma genitalium infection is 20 times more likely in men with persistent or recurrent urethritis compared to those without. The accuracy of syndromic management algorithms and diagnostic tests varies. Flowcharts used in syndromic management have low sensitivity and specificity, while molecular assays like GeneXpert® demonstrate high sensitivity (95%) and specificity (98%). Hypothetical point-of-care tests show moderate accuracy, with sensitivity and specificity ranging from 80% to 90%. The balance of benefits and harms favors molecular testing or treating all cases empirically. Syndromic management often results in missed cases or unnecessary treatment, whereas molecular testing ensures accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment. In high-prevalence settings, treating all individuals with urethral discharge for gonorrhea and chlamydia is acceptable, despite the risk of overtreatment, as it reduces complications and transmission. Cost-effectiveness analyses indicate that syndromic management and treating all cases are less expensive than molecular testing. Treating all cases costs approximately $1,660 per 1,000 men with urethral discharge, slightly more than syndromic management but with no missed cases. Molecular testing, while more accurate, incurs higher costs, with GeneXpert® costing around $17,000 per 1,000 men. In settings with limited or no molecular testing capacity, syndromic treatment is recommended to ensure same-day treatment. Good clinical practice includes taking a detailed medical and sexual history, performing a physical examination, and offering HIV and syphilis testing along with other preventive services. For settings with access to quality-assured molecular testing, the following recommendations are made: 1. Perform molecular assays (e.g., NAAT) to confirm or exclude Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. 2. Treat based on test results on the same day. 3. If tests are negative but urethral discharge persists, treat for non-gonococcal and non-chlamydial urethritis, such as Mycoplasma genitalium or Trichomonas vaginalis. 4. For recurrent or persistent urethral discharge, repeat molecular assays after 21 days and test for antimicrobial-resistant pathogens. In cases where same-day molecular testing is not feasible, syndromic treatment should be provided for gonorrhea and chlamydia, with test results used later to guide partner management. Persistent or recurrent cases should be referred to facilities with laboratory capacity for comprehensive diagnosis and antimicrobial resistance testing. Microscopy does not significantly improve the sensitivity or specificity of syndromic management algorithms. Studies highlight variability in the implementation of syndromic approaches, and a simplified management strategy may enhance adherence to guidelines. Molecular testing remains the most effective method for ensuring correct treatment, particularly in high-prevalence populations. In conclusion, while molecular testing is the gold standard for managing urethral discharge, syndromic management remains a viable alternative in resource-limited settings. Treating all cases empirically is cost-effective and ensures no missed infections, particularly in high-prevalence areas.
